title: Thermal runaway protection triggered
shortDescription: Printer detected abnormal hotend or bed temperature change and halted to prevent fire.
fullDescription:
Thermal runaway is a critical safety feature in Marlin firmware. When the measured temperature deviates from the target by more than a set tolerance for too long, the printer immediately shuts off all heaters and stops the print. This prevents dangerous overheating that could damage the printer or cause a fire.

Common causes include a loose or damaged thermistor, a failing heater cartridge, a loose silicone sock causing airflow issues, or a PID that needs to be tuned. The error usually happens early in the heat-up phase or mid-print when heating is briefly requested.

Always investigate before resetting and reprinting — dismissing thermal runaway without diagnosis is unsafe.

causes.cause: Loose or damaged thermistor wire on hotend
Heater cartridge failing or undersized for ambient temp
PID values not tuned for current hardware
Missing silicone sock — too much heat loss

fixSteps.title: Power off and inspect thermistor
fixSteps.instruction: Unplug the printer. Remove the silicone sock and visually inspect the thermistor wires for breaks or loose crimps at the hotend.

fixSteps.title: Reseat or replace thermistor
fixSteps.instruction: Push the thermistor fully into the heater block and secure with the set screw. Replace if damaged (~$5).

fixSteps.title: Install silicone sock
fixSteps.instruction: Fit a new silicone sock over the heater block to reduce heat loss and stabilize readings.

fixSteps.title: Run PID autotune
fixSteps.instruction: Connect via Pronterface/OctoPrint and send M303 E0 S210 C8, then save with M500.

whenToCallPro: If you are uncomfortable opening the hotend or the heater cartridge terminal looks damaged, contact a repair shop.

faq.q: Is it safe to disable thermal runaway?
faq.a: No. Never disable thermal runaway — it is the only firmware protection against fire.

faq.q: Why does it happen only at print start?
faq.a: Initial heat-up has the steepest temperature ramp, which exposes loose thermistors first.

title: Minimum temperature error
shortDescription: Thermistor reads below the minimum allowed temperature, indicating a broken or disconnected sensor.
fullDescription:
MINTEMP appears when the hotend or bed thermistor reports a value lower than the firmware-configured minimum (usually 5°C). This almost always means the thermistor wire is broken, unplugged, or the connector on the mainboard has come loose.

The firmware intentionally refuses to heat when it cannot trust the temperature reading, because running a heater without feedback would damage the printer.

Check continuity of the thermistor and the mainboard connection before replacing parts.

fixSteps.title: Check thermistor connector
fixSteps.instruction: Open the control box and reseat the TH0 (hotend) and TB (bed) connectors on the mainboard.

fixSteps.title: Test thermistor resistance
fixSteps.instruction: At room temperature a working 100k thermistor reads ~100kΩ. Use a multimeter on the two thermistor pins.

fixSteps.title: Replace thermistor
fixSteps.instruction: Install a new 100k NTC cartridge thermistor, route the wire carefully and secure with cable ties.

whenToCallPro: If the thermistor connector on the mainboard is burnt or damaged.

faq.a: Yes, garages below 5°C can cause false MINTEMP at power-on. Warm the printer first.

title: Maximum temperature exceeded
shortDescription: Thermistor reports a temperature higher than the firmware limit, usually from a shorted thermistor.
fullDescription:
MAXTEMP indicates the temperature sensor is reading above the firmware's safety ceiling (typically 275°C hotend, 125°C bed). It normally means the thermistor has shorted to ground or the wire insulation has melted and wires have fused.

This is the opposite failure of MINTEMP — firmware cuts power to prevent actual overheating from the stuck-on heater.

Inspect for burnt insulation near the heater block before testing.

causes.cause: Shorted thermistor wire near heater block

symptoms: Temperature briefly shows very high value

fixSteps.title: Inspect wire insulation
fixSteps.instruction: Look for melted insulation at the point where the thermistor wire enters the heater block.

fixSteps.title: Replace thermistor
fixSteps.instruction: Install a new thermistor and route the new wire away from the heater block using PTFE sleeving.

whenToCallPro: If the mainboard fuse blew or TH0 pin is damaged.

faq.a: Potentially. The heater may have reached unsafe temperatures — inspect the heater block for discoloration.

title: SD card initialization failed
shortDescription: Printer cannot read the inserted SD card.
fullDescription:
The LCD firmware expects a FAT32-formatted SD card of 32GB or less with short (8.3) filenames. Larger cards, exFAT format, or corrupted partitions cause initialization to fail silently or with an explicit error.

A worn SD card slot with bent contacts is also common — Creality's stock slots are fragile.

Reformatting the card usually fixes the issue; replacing the card reader is the next step.

causes.cause: Card formatted exFAT instead of FAT32

fixSteps.title: Reformat card as FAT32
fixSteps.instruction: Use a computer to format the SD card FAT32 with 4096-byte allocation. Reload gcode files.

fixSteps.title: Try smaller card
fixSteps.instruction: Use an 8GB or 16GB Class 10 card known to work with Creality.

fixSteps.title: Inspect SD slot
fixSteps.instruction: Look at the card reader contacts with a flashlight. Straighten bent pins with a needle.

whenToCallPro: If the LCD itself is broken or the ribbon cable is damaged.
videoSearchQuery: Creality Ender 3 SD card not working fix

faq.q: Why does my 64GB card not work?
faq.a: Marlin SD library only supports up to 32GB FAT32. Use a smaller card.

title: Filament runout sensor triggered
shortDescription: Printer paused because the filament runout sensor reports no filament.
fullDescription:
Creality printers with an optical or mechanical runout sensor pause the print when filament is no longer detected. Sometimes the sensor triggers falsely due to a stuck lever, broken microswitch, or the filament slipping past the sensor without pushing the lever.

Check the sensor cable continuity and verify that the lever moves freely when filament passes through.

fixSteps.title: Load new filament
fixSteps.instruction: Feed fresh filament through the sensor until it clicks, then resume the print.

fixSteps.title: Inspect sensor lever
fixSteps.instruction: Open the sensor housing and check that the lever springs back freely.

fixSteps.title: Test sensor cable
fixSteps.instruction: Use a multimeter in continuity mode to test the sensor cable at both ends.

whenToCallPro: Rarely needed — this is a user-serviceable sensor.

faq.a: Yes, via M412 S0 in Marlin, but you lose runout protection.

title: Automatic bed leveling probe failed
shortDescription: Printer could not complete the mesh bed leveling sequence.
fullDescription:
Automatic Bed Leveling (ABL) with CR Touch or BLTouch probes the bed at multiple points. If any probe fails — because the probe didn't deploy, the bed is too far, or the Z-offset is wrong — leveling aborts and the error is shown.

Common causes include a BLTouch pin that won't extend, a bed that is too low at the corners to reach the probe, or mounting the probe too high above the nozzle tip.

causes.cause: BLTouch pin stuck or alarm state
Bed too far from nozzle for probe to reach

fixSteps.title: Clear BLTouch alarm
fixSteps.instruction: Send M280 P0 S160 via terminal to reset the probe.

fixSteps.title: Manually raise bed
fixSteps.instruction: Level all four corners with paper so the bed is close enough for the probe to trigger.

fixSteps.title: Re-check probe mount
fixSteps.instruction: Probe pin tip should be 1-3mm below the nozzle when deployed.

whenToCallPro: If the probe hardware needs replacement and you are not comfortable with firmware configuration.
videoSearchQuery: Creality BLTouch bed leveling failed fix

faq.a: Flashing red indicates alarm state — send M280 P0 S160 to reset.

title: BLTouch probe error
shortDescription: BLTouch probe hardware or wiring fault detected.
fullDescription:
The BLTouch uses a push-pin and Hall sensor to detect the bed. Wiring faults, bent pins, or firmware mismatches cause it to enter a permanent alarm state. A healthy BLTouch blinks red once on power-up, then stays solid.

Check that the 5-pin connector is oriented correctly — swapped servo and probe wires cause instant alarm.

fixSteps.title: Check wiring polarity
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm black/red on servo header and white/black/brown on probe header match pinout diagram.

fixSteps.title: Straighten bent pin
fixSteps.instruction: If the pin does not retract smoothly, gently straighten with tweezers.

fixSteps.title: Replace probe
fixSteps.instruction: If all checks pass, install a new BLTouch/CR Touch (~$40).

whenToCallPro: If firmware flashing is required and you have not done it before.

faq.q: Can I test BLTouch without a printer?
faq.a: Yes — power it with 5V and send servo commands through a microcontroller.

title: Stepper driver overcurrent / overheat
shortDescription: TMC stepper driver shut down due to overcurrent or overtemperature.
fullDescription:
Silent stepper drivers (TMC2208/2209) on newer Creality boards report overcurrent or overtemperature faults and disable the motor until the fault clears. This usually means the Vref is set too high, the heatsink fell off, or the driver fan died.

Motors suddenly lose torque mid-print and the axis stalls — a classic symptom of driver thermal shutdown.

causes.cause: Vref set too high for driver

fixSteps.title: Verify mainboard fan
fixSteps.instruction: Open the control box and confirm the mainboard cooling fan spins at power-on.

fixSteps.title: Check Vref
fixSteps.instruction: For TMC2209 on X/Y/E set Vref to approximately 0.8V with a multimeter on the driver testpoint.

fixSteps.title: Replace heatsink
fixSteps.instruction: Use thermal tape to stick a new aluminum heatsink onto the driver chip.

whenToCallPro: If the driver chip is already burnt — mainboard swap is likely.

faq.q: Can a stalled motor damage the driver?
faq.a: TMC drivers have overcurrent protection, but repeated stalls shorten lifespan.

title: Layer shifting during print
shortDescription: Print layers offset from each other during printing.
fullDescription:
Layer shift is a visible print defect, not a true error code, but it is the most common user-reported failure. It happens when the X or Y axis loses steps — the nozzle collides, the belt slips, or the driver overheats and skips — causing every subsequent layer to be offset.

Mechanical causes (loose belts, pulleys) are more common than electrical (driver currents).

causes.cause: Nozzle catching on previous layer warp

fixSteps.title: Tighten belts
fixSteps.instruction: Belts should feel firm when plucked — not slack. Adjust the belt tensioner on X and Y.

fixSteps.title: Check pulley grub screws
fixSteps.instruction: Ensure the stepper pulley grub screw is tight on the flat of the motor shaft.

fixSteps.title: Reduce print speed
fixSteps.instruction: Drop travel speed to 100 mm/s and acceleration to 500 mm/s² to rule out missed steps.

whenToCallPro: Rarely needed — this is almost always user-fixable.

faq.q: Can layer shift resolve by itself?
faq.a: No. Once shifted, the offset is permanent for the rest of the print.

title: Extruder delivering too little plastic
shortDescription: Prints have gaps, thin walls, or missing layers due to insufficient extrusion.
fullDescription:
Under-extrusion produces visible gaps, stringy tops, and weak walls. Causes include a partial nozzle clog, a slipping extruder gear, worn Bowden PTFE tube, or E-steps that need calibration.

Start with a cold pull to clear the nozzle, then check extruder tension before adjusting slicer flow rate.

causes.cause: PTFE tube worn at hotend end

fixSteps.title: Cold pull
fixSteps.instruction: Heat to 220°C, push filament, cool to 90°C, pull out — repeat until the tip comes out clean.

fixSteps.title: Check extruder tension
fixSteps.instruction: Adjust the extruder spring tension so the gear grips but doesn't flatten the filament.

fixSteps.title: Replace PTFE tube
fixSteps.instruction: Cut a fresh square end on Capricorn tubing and re-seat fully into the hotend.

fixSteps.title: Calibrate E-steps
fixSteps.instruction: Mark 120mm of filament, extrude 100mm, measure remaining, adjust E-steps with M92.

faq.a: Clicking means the extruder gear is skipping because the nozzle is partly blocked.

title: Z-axis binding or uneven motion
shortDescription: Z-axis moves unevenly, causing banding or stalls.
fullDescription:
Single Z-axis Creality printers are prone to binding when the lead screw is misaligned or the Z-coupler is not straight. Symptoms include grinding at layer change, Z banding on prints, or a Z motor that stalls during homing.

A flexible coupler and properly aligned lead screw resolve most cases.

causes.cause: Lead screw misaligned at top bracket
Rigid coupler — needs replacing with flex coupler

fixSteps.title: Loosen top Z bracket
fixSteps.instruction: Loosen the top bracket and let the lead screw self-align while running the Z axis up and down.

fixSteps.title: Lubricate lead screw
fixSteps.instruction: Apply PTFE grease along the full length of the lead screw.

fixSteps.title: Install flex coupler
fixSteps.instruction: Replace rigid coupler with a spider-style flexible coupler to absorb lead screw wobble.

faq.q: Do I need a dual-Z upgrade?
faq.a: Not for basic binding — a flex coupler and alignment solve most cases.

title: X-axis crashed into endstop
shortDescription: X carriage ran into the frame because endstop did not trigger.
fullDescription:
During homing, the printer moves X toward the endstop. If the endstop does not trigger — broken switch, wire, or misaligned tab — the carriage crashes into the frame and the driver stalls.

Power off immediately when you hear grinding to avoid damaging the belt or motor.

fixSteps.title: Test endstop manually
fixSteps.instruction: Send M119 via terminal; press the switch by hand and watch the status change.

fixSteps.title: Re-seat endstop cable
fixSteps.instruction: Unplug and reseat the endstop connector on the mainboard.

fixSteps.title: Replace endstop switch
fixSteps.instruction: Install a new microswitch endstop module.

whenToCallPro: If the belt or motor shaft was damaged during the crash.

faq.q: Can I run M119 without printing?
faq.a: Yes — it just reports endstop status.

title: Endstop triggered unexpectedly
shortDescription: An axis endstop shows triggered when it should not be.
fullDescription:
If an endstop reports triggered at power-on, Marlin refuses to move the axis. This happens from a stuck switch, a short in the endstop cable, or noise pickup on long ribbon cables.

Run M119 to identify which endstop is stuck. Physical inspection of the switch and cable usually resolves it.

fixSteps.title: Run M119
fixSteps.instruction: Send M119 via USB terminal and identify the triggered endstop.

fixSteps.title: Inspect switch and cable
fixSteps.instruction: Look for a pressed switch, pinched cable, or loose connector.

faq.a: OPEN = switch not pressed; TRIGGERED = switch pressed.

title: Firmware flash failed
shortDescription: Printer failed to flash new firmware from SD card or USB.
fullDescription:
Creality firmware is flashed by placing a renamed .bin file on the SD card and power-cycling, or through a bootloader over USB. Common failures include wrong .bin for the hardware revision, filename identical to a previously flashed file, or a corrupted download.

Always rename the .bin to something unique (e.g., include a timestamp) so the bootloader treats it as new.

causes.cause: Same filename as last flash — bootloader ignores

fixSteps.title: Identify mainboard revision
fixSteps.instruction: Open the control box lid and read the silkscreen (4.2.2 vs 4.2.7 vs CR Touch).

fixSteps.title: Rename .bin file
fixSteps.instruction: Rename the firmware file with a unique suffix (e.g., firmware-v1.bin → firmware-v1-today.bin).

fixSteps.title: Flash
fixSteps.instruction: Place renamed .bin alone on a FAT32 SD card, power on the printer, wait 30 seconds.

whenToCallPro: If bootloader is bricked and ST-Link recovery is needed.

faq.q: Does the LCD need its own firmware?
faq.a: Yes — DWIN LCDs use a separate .TFT file. Keep both flashes consistent.

title: Wi-Fi / Sonic Pad connection lost mid-print
shortDescription: Sonic Pad or Wi-Fi link to printer dropped during a print.
fullDescription:
The Creality Sonic Pad runs Klipper over a USB link to the printer, and uses Wi-Fi for remote control. If the Pad loses Wi-Fi, remote monitoring stops but the print keeps running. If the USB link drops, the print actually aborts.

Check USB cable quality (many shipped cables are marginal), router 2.4GHz vs 5GHz channel, and Sonic Pad temperature.

causes.cause: Wi-Fi router on 5GHz only — Sonic Pad needs 2.4GHz

symptoms: Cannot reach pad from phone app

fixSteps.title: Swap USB cable
fixSteps.instruction: Use a short, shielded, high-quality USB cable between Sonic Pad and printer.

fixSteps.title: Enable 2.4GHz network
fixSteps.instruction: Configure your router with a separate 2.4GHz SSID and connect the pad there.

fixSteps.title: Cool Sonic Pad
fixSteps.instruction: Move the pad out of enclosures, add a small fan if ambient exceeds 30°C.

affectedModels: Creality Sonic Pad paired with Ender 3 S1, Ender 5 S1
whenToCallPro: If the Sonic Pad Wi-Fi module has hardware damage.
videoSearchQuery: Creality Sonic Pad WiFi disconnect fix

faq.q: Does the print stop if Wi-Fi drops but USB stays?
faq.a: No. The print continues — only remote viewing stops.
